title: Archivists
description: Appraise, edit, and direct safekeeping of permanent records and historically valuable documents. Participate in research activities based on archival materials.
tasks: Organize archival records and develop classification systems to facilitate access to archival materials.
Provide reference services and assistance for users needing archival materials.
Prepare archival records, such as document descriptions, to allow easy access to information.
Create and maintain accessible, retrievable computer archives and databases, incorporating current advances in electronic information storage technology.
Establish and administer policy guidelines concerning public access and use of materials.
Direct activities of workers who assist in arranging, cataloguing, exhibiting, and maintaining collections of valuable materials.
Preserve records, documents, and objects, copying records to film, videotape, audiotape, disk, or computer formats as necessary.
Research and record the origins and historical significance of archival materials.
Locate new materials and direct their acquisition and display.
Authenticate and appraise historical documents and archival materials.
Coordinate educational and public outreach programs, such as tours, workshops, lectures, and classes.
Specialize in an area of history or technology, researching topics or items relevant to collections to determine what should be retained or acquired.
Select and edit documents for publication and display, applying knowledge of subject, literary expression, and presentation techniques.

role_contexts.Telephone Conversations: Once a week or more but not every day
role_contexts.Contact With Others: Contact with others most of the time

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to rescue what others discard—to prove that the overlooked, the fragmentary, and the inconveniently complex deserve permanence and care.
psychological_profile.decision_style: Under uncertainty, they defer action until more context can be gathered, often consulting physical evidence or documentary trails rather than trusting verbal assurances; when forced to decide quickly, they default to preserving options rather than committing, choosing the path that keeps the most material recoverable for future reconsideration.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They notice provenance, wear patterns, and material degradation before content or meaning—an object's journey through hands and time interests them more than its current utility; they overlook or dismiss immediate emotional reactions to materials, treating sentiment as noise that obscures authentic historical signal.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: When disagreeing, they retreat into documentary evidence, presenting records rather than arguing positions, which others experience as cold or evasive; conflict carries the emotional cost of feeling misread as bureaucratic when they are being principled, deepening their withdrawal into solitary verification.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: Risk-averse regarding physical loss or irreversible alteration of materials, but risk-tolerant regarding professional reputation and institutional standing when those threaten proper stewardship.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to the role of witness rather than participant—present in groups but positioned at an angle, useful but not central, maintaining enough distance to observe without being absorbed; when no role is assigned, they become the person who remembers what others forget, accumulating unclaimed responsibility.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They negotiate with hierarchy through appeals to precedent and documented procedure, treating rules as living evidence to be interpreted rather than followed or broken.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First emotional reaction is a sense of personal betrayal by the materials themselves—their fragility feels like broken trust; second response is exhaustive documentation of the failure, creating a record so detailed that future failures might be prevented, sometimes at the cost of moving forward.
value_hierarchy: material survival of the record over interpretive clarity
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate how much future users will value comprehensive preservation and underestimate how much present users need immediate, simplified access.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They need others to eventually care about what they have saved, yet they resent the ways those others will inevitably misunderstand, simplify, or misuse the materials.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not destroy or permanently remove access to materials to solve present problems, even when every stakeholder including colleagues beg for expedient disposal.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat historical materials as raw material for their current narrative, cherry-picking and decontextualizing to serve an argument rather than encountering the past on its own terms.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They distrust the virtue of transparency—believing that unmediated access often damages what it claims to serve, and that gatekeeping can be an act of care rather than control.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When things go wrong, they blame the last person who handled the materials without documenting what they did—the invisible hand that altered the record and vanished.
